aspects.says: A cache may race only when every thread computes the same value from immutable input and stores it in one write that can't tear; a racy recomputation then costs only time.
basis: section:A Race Is Benign Only When Every Thread Writes the Same Value, in One Indivisible Write, Read Once

aspects.says: The JMM says, for each read, which writes it may return; a test run shows only what one JIT did on one CPU, not everything the model allows.
basis: section:The JMM Says Which Writes a Read May Return, and a Test Shows Only Some of Them

aspects.says: A lazily cached mutable object is not a benign race: other threads can see it before it is complete, and a change made through it reaches every caller.
basis: section:A Race Is Benign Only When Every Thread Writes the Same Value, in One Indivisible Write, Read Once

aspects.says: A plain long or double may be written as two 32-bit halves, so a reader can see a value no thread wrote; volatile long and double and references are always atomic.
basis: section:A Plain long or double May Be Read Half Old, Half New

aspects.says: A program without data races behaves as an interleaving of its threads' actions, which does not make a check and the write that depends on it one step.
basis: section:A Program Without Data Races Runs as Some Interleaving of Its Threads

aspects.says: Two reads of one plain field may see writes out of order, so a lazy cache that tests its field and then returns it may return the default value; it reads the field once into a local.
basis: section:The JMM Says Which Writes a Read May Return, and a Test Shows Only Some of Them

aspects.says: Concurrency failures are visibility, ordering or atomicity failures; data races cause the first two, and atomicity failures happen in race-free programs too.
basis: section:Every Failure Here Is One of Three Kinds, and Each Has Its Unit
